assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based framework and the evidence on skill-biased technical change, polarization and import-competition shocks changed how economists and policymakers understand wage inequality and labour-demand adjustment. The work is conceptually clear, empirically credible, widely replicated and has large policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Autor and Katz anchor the technology, tasks and wage-structure line. Hanson is central to the trade-shock evidence, jointly with Autor and Dorn. Dorn is a close contributor, but a three-person limit forces a choice. Katz's other contributions (including mobility work) strengthen his case.
assessment.maturity: The core papers date from roughly 1992 to 2016, with decades of follow-up, robustness work and debate. This is mature, and its influence on research and public debate is well established.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would see technology and trade as one coherent discovery, or prefer to split them.
Dorn's exclusion is a judgement call within the three-name limit.
Part of the 'tasks' framework overlaps with already-recognised work by others; I rely on recall, not source checking.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Collateral constraints and credit cycles gave macroeconomics a core mechanism for how financial frictions amplify and propagate shocks. It underlies much modern analysis of financial crises and macroprudential policy.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint amplification model. Gertler is central to the financial-accelerator and quantitative macro-finance extension. Bernanke is already a laureate, so the accelerator credit is partly absorbed. Gilchrist is a significant empirical contributor but less foundational.
assessment.maturity: The work is nearly three decades old and has been confirmed repeatedly, especially after 2008. It is mature and timely.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize on banking and crises may reduce the committee's appetite for another macro-finance award.
Credit for the accelerator is shared with an existing laureate, so the third-name choice could be contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities and interest-rate rules is the working paradigm of central-bank analysis. It has very high practical and scientific influence.
assessment.attribution: Attribution is hard because many people contributed. Woodford gave the synthesis and welfare-based policy foundation, Gali the empirical and theoretical development of the NKPC and monetary transmission, and Taylor the policy rule. Calvo, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler are also strong contenders, so any trio will leave out major contributors.
assessment.maturity: The work is mature, dating from the 1980s to the 2000s, with extensive empirical use. The framework is also under challenge from heterogeneous-agent models, but that does not reduce the achievement.
uncertainties: Credit is diffuse and the three-name limit makes selection contentious.
Recent inflation episodes have prompted debate about how well the framework performs.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reshaped trade theory and empirics by explaining exporter premia, intra-industry reallocation and new channels for gains from trade. Its influence on both theory and data is large.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the clear central contribution. Helpman's broader work on trade with increasing returns and firm-level models is also foundational. Redding's role is important but more as a quantitative extender.
assessment.maturity: The work is over twenty years old, with extensive empirical confirmation and incorporation into quantitative trade models.
uncertainties: Whether Helpman's contribution is better recognised here or through the trade-and-politics work in another candidate.
Whether the committee would prefer a broader trade award, since Krugman already won for new trade theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The top-income and wealth-distribution series changed measurement and public debate on inequality and tax policy. The scientific contribution is mostly measurement and data construction, with substantial influence on public economics.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez established the long-run top-income series. Zucman extended the work to wealth and offshore holdings, which is recent and more contested. Saez also appears in the optimal-taxation line.
assessment.maturity: The core work is about two decades old and widely used. Some of the wealth and offshore estimates are more recent and still debated.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of the distributional accounts and wealth-capitalization estimates.
Whether the committee treats data construction as a Nobel-level discovery.
Policy and political salience may make the case contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Formal models of present bias, self-control and reference dependence brought psychological regularities into mainstream economics. They affect the analysis of saving, consumption and policy design.
assessment.attribution: Laibson did the quasi-hyperbolic discounting models in macro and finance. Rabin did the formal psychology-and-economics synthesis. Loewenstein developed the psychological foundations and empirical evidence. Koszegi and O'Donoghue are important, and Kahneman's earlier prize partly covers the prospect-theory side.
assessment.maturity: The work is mature, with field and lab evidence, though empirical support for some specific models (for example reference-dependent preferences) is mixed.
uncertainties: The behavioural field has already been recognised (Kahneman, Thaler), so marginal recognition is less likely.
Replication and mixed evidence on some predictions.
The three-name limit omits major contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave much better measurement of intergenerational mobility and of neighbourhood and childhood-environment effects. The approach has had large influence on research and policy design, and fits the register-data tradition used in the Nordic countries.
assessment.attribution: Chetty leads the programme. Hendren and Friedman are the most prominent co-authors on mobility and neighbourhood effects. Katz is credited here but is better placed in the labour-demand line.
assessment.maturity: The work is relatively recent (about 2014 onward). Core findings are influential, but some causal claims on place effects and long-run outcomes are still being replicated and refined.
uncertainties: Maturity: the long-run causal validation is not complete.
Attribution within a large collaborative research programme.
I discount the strong policy salience when judging scientific merit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The weak-instrument and identification-robust inference literature fixed a widespread flaw in applied IV work and changed standard empirical practice, especially in applied microeconomics. It has high methodological and practical value for the credibility-revolution toolkit.
assessment.attribution: Staiger and Stock (1997) identified the weak-instruments problem and its consequences. Andrews and Moreira, with others, developed the robust tests and critical values. Yogo contributed to testing and the weak-IV literature, but with less foundational standing.
assessment.maturity: The work is mature (mostly 1990s to 2010s) and widely adopted in applied work.
uncertainties: Whether econometric-methods prizes at this level would follow soon after the 2021 award on causal inference.
Attribution is spread over many theorists.
The contribution is largely corrective and diagnostic rather than a new framework.
